## 1. Research question

::: {.slide-prompt}
State your research question and explain why it matters to the intended audience.
Identify the event, place, and time period.
:::

## 2. Study area and period

::: {.slide-prompt}
Insert your study-area map. Explain how you defined Greater Bangkok and restricted
the incident records to 2022. Include boundary source and vintage.
:::

## 3. Data and event definition

::: {.slide-prompt}
Describe your sources, observation coverage, and definition of one event.
Include the final event count only after running and checking your preparation.
:::

## 4. Data quality

::: {.slide-prompt}
Summarise your inclusion and exclusion counts. Explain the most consequential
data-quality issue and how you treated it.
:::

## 5. Analytical approach

::: {.slide-prompt}
Explain your first- and second-order methods, the null model, key parameters,
and the assumptions needed to interpret your results.
:::

## 6. First-order evidence

::: {.slide-prompt}
Insert your main intensity map or graphic with units and a readable legend.
Add your interpretation, at most 150 words, and a limitation.
:::

## 7. Second-order evidence

::: {.slide-prompt}
Insert your second-order result with the null model and distance units clearly
labelled. Add your interpretation, at most 150 words, and an inference caveat.
:::

## 8. Sensitivity and integrated findings

::: {.slide-prompt}
Show how a justified sensitivity check affects your conclusion. Connect this
evidence to your first- and second-order findings.
:::

## 9. Limitations

::: {.slide-prompt}
Explain the limitations that matter most for your conclusions. Distinguish
recorded event concentration from exposure-adjusted accident risk.
:::

## 10. Public-safety implications

::: {.slide-prompt}
Summarise your own evidence-supported implications and the additional information
needed before action. Keep these consistent with the technical report.
:::
